articles.title: Keeping the working copy on my laptop while the agent runs on a server
articles.excerpt: A refactor runs on a server while I sit on a train. I open the preview on my phone, see the page the agent just changed, type one correction, put the phone away. Two hours later I open the laptop at m…
articles.body: A refactor runs on a server while I sit on a train. I open the preview on my phone, see the page the agent just changed, type one correction, put the phone away. Two hours later I open the laptop at my desk and the work is in my working tree: new files, half-edited ones, a failing test I still have to fix. Nothing was committed, pushed or pulled. Why there are two copies A coding agent needs a machine that stays on and I need the code on the computer in front of me. Every other answer moves the code somewhere: a cloud agent clones the repository into a VM and your working copy becomes a stale checkout; tmux on a rented box keeps the agent alive and leaves the project on the server. Corami keeps a real copy of the project on both sides.

articles.title: One panic shouldn't kill the scan: isolating rules with catch_unwind
articles.excerpt: Cloud Cost Analyzer runs 92 rules against your cloud account in a single scan. A rule is a real unit of work: it pulls a resource's config and metrics, evaluates them against a cost model, and maybe e…
articles.body: Cloud Cost Analyzer runs 92 rules against your cloud account in a single scan. A rule is a real unit of work: it pulls a resource's config and metrics, evaluates them against a cost model, and maybe emits a finding. They're independent, and every one of them leans on libraries I don't control: cloud SDKs, response parsers, date and math crates. Any of that can meet an input it didn't anticipate and panic: an unwrap() that couldn't fail until some resource shape I'd never seen, an index out of bounds deep in a dependency, an overflow on a field that's normally small. Usually nobody wrote bad code. A library just hit an edge case nobody dependency-audited for. The question isn't whether a rule will panic. It's what happens to the other 91 when rule 57 does.

articles.title: A Field Guide to Beating Amazon Bedrock Throttling
articles.excerpt: If you run real LLM traffic through Amazon Bedrock, throttling is not an edge case. It is the normal operating condition at scale. A ThrottlingException or TooManyRequestsException is Bedrock telling…
articles.body: If you run real LLM traffic through Amazon Bedrock, throttling is not an edge case. It is the normal operating condition at scale. A ThrottlingException or TooManyRequestsException is Bedrock telling you that your request rate or token rate crossed a quota for that model in that region. The fix is rarely one setting. It is a layered defense: understand the quota, retry intelligently, cap concurrency, degrade gracefully, handle timeouts, and know what to escalate to AWS. This is the set of strategies I run across production LLM workloads, written as a generic guide. No workload specifics, just the patterns and when each one earns its place. TL;DR Know your quota first: check Service Quotas, learn which limits are adjustable (soft) and which are not (hard).

articles.excerpt: Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to Earth’s celestial companion a…
articles.body: Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to Earth’s celestial companion as early as November 2026. The 480-kilogram FLIP rover, short for “FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform,” is the first in a series of vehicles NASA’s contracted from Astrolab, including future buggies that will move Artemis astronauts across the moon’s surface. Fitted with deformable wheels engineered for the rugged terrain and designed to survive at least 150 hours of the frigid lunar night, FLIP will carry 20 scientific payloads including a lidar 3D mapper and a sensor to measure concentrations of the isotope helium-3 in lunar regolith.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos is playing the long game with Blue Origin (op-ed)
articles.excerpt: If Blue Origin goes public, it will have to meet the expectations of shareholders. Jeff Bezos may therefore want to establish a stronger business before committing to a listing.
articles.body: Daniel Biedermann is a partner at NewSpace Capital. He contributed this article to Space.com's Expert Voices: Op-Ed & Insights . Jeff Bezos , the founder and former CEO of Amazon, recently said that Blue Origin , his space technology company, is likely to go public in the coming years. The announcement has (unsurprisingly) attracted considerable attention, not least because Bezos has spent more than two decades financing the company largely from his personal wealth. He has invested billions of dollars in developing rockets , spacecraft and other forms of technology, often with very little prospect of an immediate return. But although Bezos has now raised the possibility of an initial public offering, he has given no firm indication of when one might happen.
articles.author: Daniel Biedermann

articles.title: A supercomputer is about to launch to the moon for the 1st time, aboard a rover named FLIP
articles.excerpt: And yes, it has AI.
articles.body: HAWTHORNE, Calif. — A moon buggy carrying a history-making supercomputer is ready to launch to the lunar surface. And it's taking some inspiration from Mars. Later this year, Astrolab will launch its uncrewed moon rover FLIP to the lunar south pole as part of the Griffin Mission 1, or Griffin-1. The California company is one of two that NASA has selected to develop a drivable rover for the agency's Artemis program. On board FLIP will be Hewlett Packard Enterprise's (HPE) Spaceborne Computer-4, an advanced computer module built to be used in space. This will be the first time that high-performance computing and artificial intelligence will be tested on the lunar surface.
